 ******************************************************************************)

native component FlatString

import String.{maxLeafSize, concatAndBalanceIfNecessary, CatString, spaces}
import Stream.{...}

export FlatString


private language="java"
private package="com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim"

lineSeparator: String = LineSeparator()

private natLineSeparator(): String = builtinPrimitive(
            "com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.Writer$LineSeparator")

private LineSeparator(): String =do
    ignore(FlatString); (* This initializes the constructor for FlatString
                   before its type is used (in the next line). *)
    natLineSeparator()
  end

object FlatString extends { String, DelegatedIndexed⟦Char, ZZ32⟧ }
    getter size() : ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Size")
    getter asExprString() : String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$ToString")
    getter asFlatString(): String = self
    getter asString(): String = self
    getter asDebugString(): String = asDebugStringIndented(0)
    getter depth():ZZ32 = 0

    (* With the help of trait DelegatedIndex, this defines our generate method *)
    getter generator() : Generator⟦Char⟧ =
        self.indices.map⟦Char⟧(fn (i:ZZ32):Char ⇒ self.get(i))

    getter isBalanced():Boolean = true
    getter isAlmostBalanced():Boolean = true
    getter isExtremelyUnbalanced():Boolean = false

    opr |self| : ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Size")

    uncheckedSubstring(r1: Range⟦ZZ32⟧) : String = do
    (* We could build a subString node here, but not until everything is working,
        because that will introduce
       SubString objects into code that may still expect FlatStrings.
       As written, this method always answers a FlatString.
       In any case, the FlatString object supports substring without copying*)
        assert((r1 ∩ self.bounds).isEmpty, r1.isEmpty,
                    "Empty substring of non-empty string")
        if r1.isEmpty then ""
        else self.javaSubstr(r1.left.get, r1.right.get + 1)    (* Java substr's endIndex is one past the last character *)
        end
    end

    opr =(self, other: FlatString): Boolean =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Eq")
    opr <(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) < 0
    opr <=(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) ≤ 0
    opr >(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) > 0
    opr >=(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) ≥ 0
    opr CMP(self, other: FlatString): TotalComparison =  self.cmp(other) CMP 0
    opr CMP(self, other:String):TotalComparison = INVERSE (other CMP self)
    opr CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP(self, other:FlatString): TotalComparison =
      self.cicmp(other) CMP 0
    opr CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP(self, other:String): TotalComparison = INVERSE (other CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP self)

    (** get skips bounds checking. **)
    get(i:ZZ32): Char =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Index")
    cmp(other:FlatString): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Cmp")
    cicmp(other:FlatString): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$CICmp")
    javaSubstr(lo:ZZ32,hi:ZZ32): String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Substr")
    javaSubstr(lo:ZZ32): String = javaSubstr(lo, self.size)
    javaIndexOf(c:Char): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$IndexOf")
    flatConcat(self, b:FlatString):String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Concat")
    flatConcat(self, b:Char):String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$Concat")
    javaRegExpMatches(m:FlatString): Boolean =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$javaRegExpMatches")
    javaRegExpSplit(m:FlatString, i:ZZ32): String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.FlatString$javaRegExpSplit")

    indexOf(c:Char): Maybe⟦ZZ32⟧ = do
        i = javaIndexOf(c)
        if i = -1 then Nothing⟦ZZ32⟧ else Just⟦ZZ32⟧(i) end
      end

    verify():() = do
        assert(self.depth, 0, self)
    end

    asDebugStringIndented(indent: ZZ32): String =
        spaces(indent) || "J" |self| "/" self.depth ":" self

    opr ∈(c:Char, self): Boolean = self.javaIndexOf(c) ≠ -1

    rangeContains(r: Range⟦ZZ32⟧, c: Char):Boolean = self.javaIndexOf(c) ∈ self.bounds[r]

    (** The operator %||% with at least one String argument converts to string and
        concatenates **)
    opr ||(self, b:FlatString): String = do
        if b.isEmpty then self
        elif self.size + b.size > maxLeafSize then
             (* Since both self and b have depth 0, balancing can't be necessary *)
            CatString(self, b)
        else
            flatConcat(self, b)
        end
      end

    opr ||(self, b:String):String = do

2	
3	# The coordinator skill's outline, and a home for every entry that leaves the record
4	
5	The `coordinator` skill is to be rewritten from scratch (`coordinator-rewrite-plan.md`; POSITIONS, "The coordinator rewrite's goals."). Before that, FACTS and POSITIONS are consolidated. The curator ruled that the two files hold the project only:
6	
7	- 09:16 UTC: "positions and facts I believe should relate to the project only. ... every other thing about working between us needs to go to the coordinator skill".
8	- 11:40 UTC: "We are not moving everything to coordinator skill, only the editing and extracting from workers' reports goes in here. The usage by workers must stay there and also the local edits when we ask them must be described there as well." ("There" is the `fortress-repo` skill.)
9	- 15:25 UTC: start by drafting the skill's outline, and assign each evicted fact and position to the right place in it, so that nothing is lost between the two systems.
10	
11	This note does that in three steps. Section 1 is the outline. Section 2 gives every entry that leaves FACTS or POSITIONS, and every point of the held list on how we work, its home. Section 3 says what that leaves the consolidation to do. Line numbers are at commit `77ab93037`. The record store's design (`record-store-design.md`, section 3.6, point 1, and section 5, decision 1) recommends numbering each entry by its line at the numbering commit; if the files are numbered as they stand now, these line numbers are the entries' numbers. Times are UTC, 2026-10-13 unless a date is given. Sizes are characters of entry lines (Python's count), K for thousands.
12	
13	Words used here:
14	
15	**core**
16	: Part of the new skill that is always loaded: at session start, after every compaction, and from then on.
17	
18	**part**
19	: Reference file of the new skill, loaded when the coordinator switches into its kind of work.
20	
21	**mode**
22	: Kind of work the coordinator switches into, such as running a batch.
23	
24	**project**
25	: The language, the library, the tree (the code and the tools that build, test and measure it), the specification, the plan, and the curator's decisions about them.
26	
27	**evicted entry**
28	: Entry of FACTS or POSITIONS that is not about the project, so it leaves the file.
29	
30	**home**
31	: Place where an evicted entry's content will stand: a section of this outline, a part of `fortress-repo`, or a part of `cloud-container`.
32	
33	**split entry**
34	: Entry that holds a project decision with a working rule inside it. The rule leaves and the rest stays.
35	
36	**borderline entry**
37	: Entry that can be read either way. Section 2.3 says why it went where it did.
38	
39	**already there**
40	: The home already states the content, so the entry needs no new text there.
41	
42	## 1. The outline
43	
44	The outline starts from the candidate modes and the shape in the plan's draft of the writer's brief (section 3, points 4 and 5) and the kept rules of point 6. Section 1.4 lists where it departs from them and why. The sizes are the plan's: the core about 10K bytes, the whole skill no longer than the 41K bytes of the skill it replaces, its sources file aside.
45	
46	### 1.1 The core
47	
48	Loaded at every session start and after every compaction. It holds what bears on any turn, whatever the coordinator is doing.
49	
50	1. **The standing goal.** Model what the curator knows and where his gaps are, and fill them with the few facts he needs to decide. Do not re-explain what he knows. This is the executive assistant's role. The profile of what he knows, once built (plan section 6, point 1), is read here.
51	2. **His role and his decisions.** He sets the goals and decides the design and process questions put to him. A bare go starts background work only; a batch needs his explicit go; a standing go covers what it names. What makes a decision consequential, and its three ways to him. A decision inside a worker's report is not made until he sees it. Search the record before asking him or measuring. A remark is not a decision. A deeper pass, not a halt or a rollback. Weigh a rule by its purpose and its cost. A proposal of the coordinator's stays marked as its own until his yes.
52	3. **Talking to him.** The register. The ask, one per message, the recommendation last. Lists, not tables; numbers as K or M; a new term defined; a choice numbered. Time read from the clock, given in UTC and his time. Costs in tokens, writes only. Silence while a batch runs. What he hears about record edits. The hook's reminders handled silently. While he reads turn by turn, restate each point in a line and hold it. Pages for him: a Select button per section, sources at the bottom, the house style, updated by URL. A push notification when he is away. No do-nothing option among the choices.
53	4. **The facts of this environment.** The facts of the plan's section 3, point 7 that bear on any turn: his iPhone, Speak and dictation; a path does not open there, a link does; his client can show stale state; his time zone; compaction; a lost container keeps only what is pushed; auto mode, the permission check and manual mode; the prompt cache's life; the platform's process stops; a message during a turn is queued, a stop kills the running agents; cached reads are almost free; the tiers, and the tier the coordinating session runs on.
54	5. **The record: what goes where.** Each home and its purpose: FACTS and POSITIONS (the project only, read in briefs), the history files, INDEX, PLAN, the boot note, the held list, the review queue, notes and reports, the gap ledger, and the skills (how we work: this skill; rules that bind workers: `fortress-repo`; the platform: `cloud-container`). One home per thing. What he says about how we work comes here, refined. Push after every commit.
55	6. **The boot.** The boot order; what is read whole and what is looked up, which the trial boot settles (decision 5); what is in flight, read from the tree; whether a worker still runs; `git log`; the boot note rewritten whole; after each start of the process, the git-check hook's reset, told to him in a line.
56	7. **The parts.** One line for each part below: what it holds and when to load it.
57	
58	### 1.2 The parts
59	
60	Each is loaded when the coordinator switches into its work. Several can be loaded at once.
61	
62	1. **Delegating: briefing, launching, watching and resuming agents.** The briefer of workers. Loaded before the coordinator briefs, launches, watches, resumes or relaunches any agent, in any mode, a batch's agents included. It holds the tiers, the Fable rule and the all-models pool; what a brief holds (the problem and not the answer, the research on file, the record's measurements as findings, the record's slice quoted and not restated, a length cap for an update, no second reader that reframes a document, no request that a worker cap its own spend); watching a long run against its estimate, with check-ins armed at launch; waits and the prompt cache; interrupts and stops of the process; resuming a run, and relaunching only at his ask; the Workflow tool's traps; headless sessions; the scope of a separate session.
63	2. **Running and reviewing a batch.** The batch coordinator. Loaded when a batch is prepared, launched, watched, landed or reviewed. It holds the go a batch needs and the standing go's sequence; the workflow script and its manual, which are in scope for improvement; the base built once and the seeded worktrees; the roles (worker, skeptic, judge) and what each checks; reversible stops, the blocking second review, tests-only repairs, and a deeper pass on a red gate; what a batch commits; the mission briefing; the checker-count and distance stages; the landing (consolidation, `revival-changes.md` updated, items listed for him); the review after every batch; resuming a batch after a stop or the limits.
64	3. **Planning the road.** The roadmap architect. Loaded when PLAN's order or a phase is in question, before a batch is briefed, and when there is idle time. It holds PLAN's phases and parked items; a fork probed before a batch is briefed; the nine steps, with the library's own way first; his answers asked in the plan's order, rows one per message; idle time given to parked research; a new deliverable discussed with him first.
65	4. **Keeping the record.** The record-keeping part of the plan's step 2 (`record-rule-draft.md`), with the tool of the record store's design (`record-store-design.md`) if he takes it. Loaded when the coordinator edits FACTS, POSITIONS, INDEX or a history file, folds a worker's report into the record, or runs a consolidation. It holds an entry's form and measure; the numbered entries; the history and its provenance; the pass after a worker finishes; the consolidation and its checks; INDEX's lines; the ledger's rewrites and derived views; a record that is public and names models on purpose. How workers read the record, and the edits a brief asks them to make, stay in `fortress-repo` (section 1.5).
66	5. **Rewriting a skill.** Loaded when a skill is to change, when the writer is briefed or resumed, when a cold read runs, and when his comments on a skill's page come in. It holds the outline first; the `fortress-repo` method, and the heavier method of this rewrite; the seven writing principles and the register; the headless writer; the cold read, the coordinator's review of its flags, and his reading of whole parts; a comment marks a problem area; what belongs in which skill; `revival-changes.md` kept current; a rewrite no longer than what it replaces.
67	6. **Analysis: process engineering and post-mortems.** The analyst. Loaded when the coordinator measures what the work costs or how long it takes, tests a change to the process, or finds out what happened and why. It holds where the work's costs are measured; the spend read from the transcripts' usage records; a boot's cost; the Fable ratio; the development loop; small tests on the records at hand; archaeology by Sonnet scouts; reading transcripts and Workflow journals; the post-mortem's index into a transcript; the profile of what he knows, built here as its own task.
68	
69	### 1.3 The five roles
70	
71	The goals entry names five roles that must not be lost (plan, decision 6). The executive assistant is the core. The briefer of workers is Part 1, the batch coordinator Part 2, the roadmap architect Part 3, the analyst Part 6. Parts 4 and 5 serve all five.
72	
73	### 1.4 Where it differs from the plan's candidates, and why
74	
75	1. **"Briefing and running workers outside a batch" becomes Part 1, loaded before any launch.** 18 evicted entries land there. Most of them hold for a batch's agents, a skill writer and a scout alike: the tiers and the Fable rule, what a brief holds, interrupts, resuming a run, waits and the cache, the Workflow tool's traps (POSITIONS 105, 108, 110, 117, 119; FACTS 195, 200, 201, 204 to 209). Split by "outside a batch", they would stand twice, once here and once in the batch part.
76	2. **"Process engineering" and "a post-mortem" become one part, Part 6, with two modes.** Both are the analyst's role. Both read the same sources (the transcripts and their usage records, the Workflow journals, git) with the same tools (`spend.py`, `journal-text.py`). Among the sorted entries the post-mortem has few homes of its own: the transcript index of POSITIONS 128, and the held list's points on archaeology, most of them done (`HELD.md:88`, `:97` to `:102`).
77	3. **The launch mechanics leave the core for Part 1.** The plan's point 7 puts in the core that a Workflow `agent()` can return null, that a script is checked as an async body, and how a stopped run resumes. 79	5. **Kept as the plan has it.** Talking, asking and deciding are the core, not a mode. Planning the road, rewriting a skill and running a batch are parts. 84	- **Part 4** holds the editing of FACTS and POSITIONS and the extracting from workers' reports: the entry's form, the history, the pass after a worker finishes, the consolidation.
85	- **`fortress-repo`'s `references/records.md`** keeps how workers read, query and cite the record, and how they write a fact, a ledger row or a decision when a brief asks them to.

92

It leaves if its subject is how he and the coordinator talk and decide, how agents are briefed, run and checked, how batches run, how the record is kept, how skills are written, or how the platform and the Claude Code harness behave. A rule that binds workers goes to `fortress-repo`. How the platform behaves goes to `cloud-container`.

3	# The coordinator rewrite: the plan
4	
5	This plan follows the method on record: your decision on the rewrite's goals, and your decision on how the skills are written and checked. It adds no step, rule or tool. Where the record is silent, or two entries pull different ways, it lists a decision for you with the default the record suggests.
6	
7	Times are UTC, dates 2026. A cost is tokens written. A cost marked "estimate" isn't measured. The files to open: [this plan](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/coordinator-rewrite-plan.md), [the map](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/coordinator-shape.md), [sort A](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/rule-sort.md), [sort B](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/rule-sort-b.md), [the rules' origins](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/duplicated-rules-evidence.md), [the held list](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/coordinator/HELD.md).
8	
9	Words used here:
10	
11	**coordinator**
12	: Session that talks to you, briefs the workers and keeps the record.
13	
14	**record**
15	: Files under `explorations/` that hold the project's memory: FACTS (what's established), POSITIONS (your decisions), INDEX (one line per note), PLAN (the working plan), the boot note (what's in flight), the held list (your points held while you read) and the history files.

36	: Reading of a rewritten skill by a fresh Opus agent given only the skill. It flags what would send its reader wrong or make it search, and edits nothing.

3	# The conduct rules against the baseline
4	
5	The `coordinator` skill is being rewritten on Pavol's principle: the skill holds only what the model wouldn't do by itself. A rule that restates the model's own habit is clutter.
6	
7	To find those habits, fresh sessions of Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 answered eighteen questions about the coordinator's job, one question per turn, with no record and no skill. They were given the setting and nothing else. The setting says they coordinate workers from a cloud container for weeks, that the owner reads on a phone with text-to-speech and dictates, that their context gets compacted, and that the container can be lost.
8	
9	This note sorts every conduct rule on record against those answers. A conduct rule is a rule about how the coordinator works: how it talks to Pavol, how it asks and decides, how it delegates, how it keeps the record and how it runs agents. The list I sorted is the 73 rules in six groups in `coordinator-shape.md`, section 4.1. I cite the answers as F for Fable 5.1 and O for Opus 5.5 with the question number. So (F4, O12) means Fable's answer to question 4 and Opus's answer to question 12.
10	
11	Each rule goes in one of five buckets.
12	
13	- **Default.** Both models do it by themselves, so the rule is dropped from the skill.
14	- **Environment.** This environment needs it, so it's kept. The environment here is the phone and dictation, compaction, a container that can be lost, the harness (Claude Code and its tools) and Pavol's right to decide.
15	- **Project.** This project needs it, so it's kept. These are the project's methods, its workflow and its record.
16	- **Workers.** The rule binds worker agents. It belongs in `fortress-repo`, the skill every worker loads, not in the coordinator's.
17	- **State.** It isn't a rule. It's a fact about the current setup, such as a machine limit or a quirk of a tool.
18	
19	Two things to keep in mind while reading the sort.
20	
21	First, an interview shows what a model says it would do, not what it does. Pavol accepted that limit when he chose the method. It matters most for a rule written in many places, because a rule usually gets written again after the coordinator breaks it. Where such a rule lands in the default bucket, I say so.
22	
23	Second, the models answered knowing the setting. Several rules follow from a fact in the setting, and the models worked them out for themselves. So the skill can often drop a rule and state the fact behind it instead. That's taken up after the sort.
24	
25	I had only each rule's one-line name from the inventory and read no other place where it's written. Where a name leaves the rule's scope open, the reason below says how I read it.

And both list two or three numbered choices when they put a document to him (F10, O10). So the default bundles asks, which the rule doesn't allow.

Neither says what a yes commits him to and what a no costs when it asks a design question, though both come near it for a document (F10, O10). 236	## The shape of the skill
237	
238	The buckets suggest a skill in three layers.
239	
240	The first layer is a short opening of facts, always loaded. It covers who Pavol is and how he reads and dictates, his time zone, compaction and the container, where the record keeps what, the tiers, and the harness's signals and quirks. These facts replace the 7 state items, and they're what lets most of the 15 defaults go without a reminder.
241	
242	The second layer is a few principles, also always loaded, built from the environment rules about Pavol. The standing goal comes first (rule 16). Then his right to decide (rules 17, 21, 22, 26 and 36), and how to talk and ask (rules 1 to 6 and 10 to 14). That's 17 of the 24 environment rules, and they turn into a handful of principles rather than 17 lines. Rule 25, on purposes and costs, may frame the whole layer.
243	
244	The third layer is the modes, each loaded when the coordinator switches into that kind of work. The other 15 project rules sort cleanly into modes, so none of them needs to sit in the core.
245	
246	- Running a batch and its agents: rules 39, 40, 46 and 54 to 57 from the environment bucket.
247	- Briefing workers: rules 30 to 35 and 37.
248	- Keeping the record: rules 43 and 49 to 52.
249	- Rewriting skills: rules 41 and 42.
250	- Reviewing work and handling trouble: rule 24.
251	
252	The 15 defaults get no text, unless Pavol keeps a line for the two most-written ones. The 11 worker rules move to `fortress-repo`, and test first goes there only as its two differences from the default.
253	
254	So the coordinator's own text comes down from 73 rules to 40, and only about 18 of those are always loaded.

185	**16.** **I wouldn't sit and watch it.** I'd start it in the background, writing progress to a log file. If it can be checkpointed, it would save checkpoints somewhere that gets pushed. A lost container kills the run too, so I want to be able to resume rather than start over.
186	
187	Before doing anything else, the status file gets an entry: what's running, why, started when, expected finish in his time, how to check on it, and the exact command to restart it. Then I push.
188	
189	While it runs, I get on with other work. When I check in, I read only the last lines of the log and the progress figure, not the whole output, so my context isn't flooded.
190	
191	**He hears from me three times at most:**
192	
193	- **At the start, in a few sentences:** what's running, roughly when it should finish and on what basis, and what I'm doing meanwhile.
194	- **If something goes wrong:** right away, with what I'm doing about it.
195	- **At the end:** the result, or a short heads-up if it's running well past the estimate.
196	
197	Otherwise I stay quiet unless he asks. As before, I can't wake myself up. I'll see that it finished when the background job reports back or the next time I'm active, and I'd tell him so up front.
198	
199	**17.** **First, find out what survived.**
200	
201	1. Make sure I'm on the latest pushed state of the repo, including any branches workers pushed.
202	2. Read CLAUDE.md, the status file in full, and the git log since the last few commits.
203	3. Check the inbox for any message from him I hadn't fully filed or acted on.
204	
205	**Then work out what was lost.** Anything not pushed is gone. Every run or worker listed as active in the status file is now dead. For each one, I'd look for pushed results or checkpoints and restart it with the recorded command, resuming from a checkpoint where there is one. Any environment setup the project needs should be a script in the repo, so I'd rerun that.
206	
207	**Then tell him, in a few sentences:** the container was lost, what survived, what was lost since roughly when, what I'm restarting, and which promised times slip and to when.
208	
209	Then I'd update the status file and push before carrying on. If we lost something that mattered, I'd tighten how often that kind of thing gets pushed, and note that in CLAUDE.md.
210	
211	**18.** Whether I do it or a worker does, the order is the same:
212	
213	1. **Read first.** The code I'm changing, its tests, and git history for why it is the way it is. Old code often looks wrong for a reason.
214	2. **Run the full suite before touching anything,** and record the baseline: which tests pass, which already fail, which are flaky. Otherwise I can't tell what I broke from what was already broken.
215	3. **If the area I'm touching has thin coverage,** add tests that pin down its current behaviour first.
216	4. **Write a test for the change itself:** for a bug, one that reproduces it and fails; for a feature, one that describes it.
217	5. **Make the smallest change that does the job,** in the style of the surrounding code. No drive-by refactoring.
218	6. **Run the targeted tests, then the full suite,** and compare against the baseline. Any new failure is mine until proven otherwise.
219	7. **Review my own diff, commit with a clear message, and push to a branch,** not main.
220	8. **Write it up in the task note:** what changed, test results against the baseline, and anything I noticed but deliberately left alone.
221	
222	If tests fail at the end, I say so and include the output, rather than calling it done.

1	<!-- What Pavol has decided, holds or already knows, as it stands now: each position in plain words, what we do and why, under a bold title that is its handle; a quote only where his words are the position itself. Timeless: no dates, no provenance, no account of how a position was reached. That record is `POSITIONS-history.md`, where every earlier text of every entry stands verbatim with what became of it. A position he has replaced is gone from here and the later one stands; a decision not yet built keeps the detail the coming work needs. A worker or a coordinator may add an entry with a date or a quote in it; the next consolidation compiles that out into the history and leaves the position. Standing directives about how we work are in `explorations/protocol.md`, and what is established is in `FACTS.md`; neither is repeated here. Read whole at session start, so that none of it is re-asked or re-explained. -->
2	
3	# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground
4	
5	## The goal
6	
7	- **The measuring stick.** Finish what the designers intended, judged by the specification in `Specification/`, the Working Draft of 2010-12 as the revival revises it, with the 2012 Types chapter cited beside it; not redesign the language. The measure is one program, microGPT, compiled to bytecode and running fast. A pure-Java microGPT is written later as the floor to measure against. The specification is a living document that reflects the changes we make. The tree is tagged `sealed-tree` at the map's last commit; commits after it edit the original sources, test-driven.
8	- **How he weighs his calls where the designers left no word.** "I don't care about type theoretical purity and I'm accepting all unfinished corners of the language because I want to get to a compiled version of micro GPT. And I think this is the right pragmatic approach so that we do not get bogged down in weeds. Theory. We want to get this one program running fast. That's our guiding star. But along the way, I want to stay true to the spirit of Fortress." He has not read the specification, the papers on its type system or the library, and relies on the record: "I assume those people knew much more than I do right now." The check he asked for is a thorough top-tier review of every decision of his against the designers' intent, for errors of commission and of omission (`reviews/decisions-review/evidence.md`, `judgement.md`, `popl-recheck.md`); its items are decisions below.
9	- **The readable expression.** The toy problem is microGPT and the search is for its most readable expression: "we are searching for the optimal expression of the microGPT algorithm for readability." Fortress's mathematical notation and Iverson's APL notation (with Hsu's data design for data-flow algorithms) are the two sources. The Hsu-style flat program gave "a few lumps of coal", not a diamond; the vocabulary is where any polishing happens. C4 is the APL target form; C2's tuple hyperparameter form is what a strand assignment expands to; the semicolon form is set aside.
10	- **The APL side quest is closed.** It was a curiosity, then a ladder to learn APL, then native code (not an interpreter in an interpreter) with microGPT as its target; its remaining ground (tacit, characters, nested arrays) is not pursued.
11	- **The 2D notation is a gimmick.** Fortify's mathematical rendering is "a neat gimmick, not a good idea": it encodes one perspective on a computation into the syntax, while the same mathematics can be written many ways; APL's glyph-per-transformation is the purer realisation. Presentation only, not on the path, not an argument for Fortress; no work on it unless he asks.
12	- **The type checker on interpreter programs.** He wants the checker, which runs only on the compile path, usable on interpreter programs, and considers it low-hanging fruit. It comes after the switch-over, when walk also takes the static coercions the checker inserts (the entry on walk's choice of coercions).
13	
14	## History he knows (do not re-explain)
15	
16	- **The project's end.** DARPA's HPCS did not take Sun into phase three (2006) and the project lived on at Sun Labs until 2012. His reading: they did no work on performance, "mucked around with syntax", and the promise that a sufficiently advanced compiler would later make mathematical types fast was never true; the funding was pulled for good reason.
17	- **Boxed numerics.** The compiled path is only about ten times the interpreter because numerics are boxed (`FRR64`, no `DADD`); "without unboxed doubles and arrays of doubles, what are we even doing here". The first measurement's scalar loop was an edge case microGPT never hits (literals in the loop, a `:=` accumulator); the fairer test he asked for agreed with him (FACTS § Execution model). The storage is his decision below; unboxed arithmetic is phase 6 of the plan.
18	- **Hsu's critique** of language paradigms as accidental complexity; he is "coming around to his point of view".
19	- **The third-party Java 9 port** gets no credit and no mention: "I don't wanna see them mentioned anywhere." CLAUDE.md no longer describes the tree as the port's migration grafted on the history; the other files that repeat that sentence wait for the lineage cleanup (`PLAN.md`). His plan to rename the graft-free `clean-ladder` branch to `main` was not carried out.
20	
21	## Decisions on record
22	
23	### The standard and the sources
24	
25	- **The specification stays the standard, the Types chapter beside it.** Where the Types chapter of the team's unfinished restart (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`) covers a topic, it is cited beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word: the exclusion rule as "instantiation exclusion" in its two-part form, the `covariant` modifier, `Bottom` inexpressible. "On the rule S revises, it is the designers' latest intent, and the goal is to finish what they intended."
26	- **The type group's late positions outweigh the early text.** The specification "was written in a vacuum early on", "as a wish"; "then the type group went in and tried to make it run. So they knew much more about what's feasible and what's not. The goal was performance. The specialization is a must"; "when that wish met reality, then the spec must change"; "whatever the spec was dreaming about in 2008 is irrelevant because it met hard reality". So the late, implementation-informed positions of the type group (the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the compiled tower flattened in 2009 and 2010 by Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen, Naden's 2012 write-up, the POPL 2019 paper) outweigh the specification's earlier text where they conflict, and the implementers' later word outweighs unfinished text. "We are not Naden. We know nothing here."
27	- **The library's own practice is the standard.** "all the extensions that [microGPT] invented need to go directly to the standard library in the spirit of the standard library." Exclusion "is a practice that is all over the standard library"; whoever extends the library "should study the existing parts of the Fortress library meticulously, and use those patterns for extending the standard library in the native way". No fix is designed from a reading of the specification alone or from a user-side workaround. A fork put to him names the library's own way first, and a fork resting on a rule that refuses something says what the library does instead (protocol principle 2). The lesson behind the rule: he had to find the diagonal's override shape himself ("why the fuck did I have to invent this solution?"), because the step skipped was what the library already does in the same family.
28	- **Fleshing out the standard library** is a very important task: first the `RR64`/`AdditiveGroup` mismatch (done by the flattening), then the algebraic layer (Ring, Field and what ML's matrices and tensors need) so the library's trait flavour reaches them; into the standard library itself, not a tree of our own.
29	- **Interpreter performance is irrelevant.** "interpreter of Fortress, which is hundreds times slower than the Python interpreter, is irrelevant for any performance discussions"; "we cannot judge anything performance related in Fortress while we do not have a compiler". No edit to C4 for speed, and no performance decision of any kind until microGPT runs compiled. The two microGPT programs never run in the gate ("those are too long running to be tests"); the ladder-regression stage compiles them and records the phase; when they one day run, the run goes to a separate non-gating stage.
30	- **The microGPT walk check is quick.** Under walk, the check of the model after a batch proves that its mathematics still works and that the library changes did not break it: about two forward-and-backward passes against the reference values, under one minute, never a full run of every check; the full check programs run only when asked. # The outline reviewed: right in shape, four placements to change

The outline is right in its shape. A core of seven sections and six parts match the five roles, the curator's three rulings and the plan's candidates. Every entry of FACTS and POSITIONS that leaves has a home, and every point of the held list on how we work has one. I found no part that should not exist and no part that is missing. I found three project decisions moved out that should stay in part, one fact of state put in the skill, three kept rules with no home, two rules with two homes, one held point in the wrong part, and one timing that would leave the coordinator without its rules for five steps. Line numbers are the outline's, at commit `77ab93037`. Nothing has touched FACTS or POSITIONS since, so they are current (`git log 77ab93037..HEAD` on the two files is empty). Times are UTC.

## 1. What I checked

- Every borderline entry of section 2.3 and every split entry of section 2.4, read whole: POSITIONS 8, 14, 19, 27, 31, 32, 33, 39, 61, 87, 123, 124, 125, 132, 133, 135, 136; FACTS 66, 111, 190, 192, 203, 219.
- The two conduct sections of POSITIONS whole (lines 100 to 145) and the container section of FACTS whole (lines 189 to 215). That covers the ten others and more: 102 to 122, 126 to 131, 134, 140 to 145; FACTS 189, 191, 193 to 202, 204 to 215.
- The "already there" claims that the placements rest on, by grep in the named parts: `session.md` (the 270 s cap, the permission check), `committing.md` ("What to commit", "Pushing"), `exploring.md` ("The choices that are yours"), `interpreter.md` (the order that varies run to run), `tests-writing.md` ("Names, comments, citations", refusals at load), `build-and-caches.md` ("Setting up each call", the `rats` folders), `worktrees.md` (seeding), `gate.md` ("When to run it"), `records.md` (read whole), `cloud-container`'s `hooks.md` and `machine.md`. All hold. `gate.md` names neither the checker-count stage nor what a comparison masks, so those are new pieces, as the outline says.
- The held list whole, the plan whole, both sorts, and the Opus answers of the baseline interview.

## 2. What is wrong or missing

Each point gives the evidence and the fix.

1. **Two project decisions on the suites leave whole.** POSITIONS 103, "The suite's verdict is the check.", decides what a test holds: a value that matters is asserted, no expected-output files, and "none of it is offered to him again". POSITIONS 102, "Test first, the test kept.", decides how the tree is changed: a failing test first, kept in the corpus, test and fix in one commit. The outline keeps 124 and 125 because they decide what the suites hold and how they run (section 2.3). 102 and 103 are decisions of the same kind, on the same suites. They are not "working between us". The worker rules are already in `fortress-repo` (`SKILL.md`, "Rules for every task"; `tests-writing.md`). Fix: both leave in part. 102 keeps its first sentence and the one-commit sentence; the skeptic's reading of test-first from the transcript goes to Part 2. 103 keeps its first sentence and "no expected-output files; none of it is offered to him again"; "no batch compares the corpus's printed outputs, no baseline is run" goes to Part 2. Both stay in the project section the outline proposes, "The suites and the gate".
2. **A decision on the gate's stages leaves whole.** POSITIONS 39, "The checker count is measured, never red.", decides that a gate stage is a measurement and that the phase-3 gates' job is driving the distance down. The outline's own definition of the project (section 2.1) names "the gate's stages as measurements". `fortress-repo` holds nothing of these stages, by POSITIONS 134, so after the move only FACTS 66 would say that the total is never red, and a fact is not his decision. Fix: 39 stays where it is, in "The one library and the compiled checker". Part 2 cites it and holds the batch's handling: `STAGE_BLIND`, the before tables, the review's tie of each risen row to a rung edit. Section 2.5 then reads 25 of 26.
3. **A fact of state goes into the core.** Core 4 would say "the coordinating session runs on Opus, and moves to Fable at his word" (POSITIONS 117). The entry itself says the tier changes at his word, and it changed on 10-12. A skill line of state goes stale at the first switch, and the boot note is the one home of state (HELD 42, decision 20). Fix: Core 4 states the tiers, that the session's tier is his to set, and his two reasons (the register, the pool). The current tier is a line of the boot note.
4. **Three kept rules have no home.** The plan's kept list (section 3, point 6) keeps "Give reading to workers. Read their reports and the record." (its failure: the repository traced by hand on 09-19), "No directory listings at boot, and every output bounded" (decision 7, kept by default), and "A go is written nowhere" (the half of "A remark isn't a decision"). None of the three appears in the outline's sections 1.1 or 1.2. They come from the protocol, not from an entry, so section 2.2 has no line for them, and the core's lines "A remark is not a decision" and "Weigh a rule by its purpose and its cost" have the same gap. Fix: Core 1 adds delegation, beside the standing goal: the coordinator's context is for him and the record; reading and long work go to workers. Core 6 adds the bounded boot. Core 2's remark line adds "a go is written nowhere". Section 1 says once that the protocol's conduct rules land by the plan's kept list, and names them where they land.
5. **Two rules have two homes.** The Workflow's mechanics (FACTS 201, 208, 209) are listed under Part 1 and Part 2 (section 2.7), and "what belongs in which skill" stands in Core 5 and in Part 5. The plan's rule is one home per thing. Fix: Part 1 holds the mechanics; Part 2 says when a batch resumes and points to Part 1. Core 5 holds the skills' split; Part 5 points to it.
6. **One held point is in the wrong part.** HELD 80, "Unsure about PLAN.md, the big plan file, as the place", is sent to Part 3 as "what PLAN holds". Its context (HELD 73 to 81) is the ledger's regrouping proposal, and "the place" is PLAN as the home of the regrouped rows. Fix: Part 4, beside HELD 81 (no go on re-deriving the views).
7. **The evicted entries leave POSITIONS too early.** Section 3.2, point 2, sends them to the history once the skill holds them and the check against the kept list (step 7) has read them. From step 7 to step 12 the coordinator still boots on the old skill and the protocol and reads POSITIONS whole; the new skill is not in use until his reading is done and the old homes are retired. For those five steps the conduct rules would be in no file the boot reads. Fix: the evicted entries leave with the protocol at step 12, "Retire the old homes", each to `POSITIONS-history.md` with one line naming its home. Decision 17 changes with it (section 4).
8. **One entry's fate is left open.** POSITIONS 61, "The separate analysis session's scope.", goes to Part 1 "if that session is over, to the history instead". Neither BOOT nor PLAN names such a session now. Fix: Part 1 holds the general rule, a second session contributes reviews and their commits on a branch of its own, not a batch or a change of route. The entry goes to the history. The consolidation checks whether the session still runs before it does.
9. **A fact about the original tree would leave FACTS.** FACTS 192 holds the leak's mechanism with its file and lines (`RatsUtil.java:138-145`, 5.8 MB each, never deleted) and sends the whole entry out on the strength of row 702. Fix: a check, not a move. Before the entry leaves, the consolidation reads row 702. If the row holds the mechanism with its lines, the entry leaves as the outline says. 10. **Section 3.3 misses four decisions the outline changes.** It names decision 23 only. Decisions 6, 17, 18 and 22 change too (section 4 below).
11. **Point 2 of the writer's brief contradicts the outline.** It gives the writer POSITIONS's conduct sections "as consolidated". The outline's section 3.2, point 2, does not rewrite them. Fix: "as they stand".

What I did not check: the README's rule sections, PLAN's three old rule sections and the boot note's standing lines. They are outside the outline's scope. The map's section 4.1 gives each of their rules its lines, and the kept list covers them. Step 12 retires them against that map.

## 3. The outline as the writer should get it

The outline's section 1 stands with the changes below folded in. Its section 2 is the map of homes, with the changed placements listed at the end of this section. The sizes are the plan's: the core about 10K bytes, the whole skill no longer than 41K bytes, the sources file aside. The protocol's conduct rules land by the plan's kept list; they are named below where they land.

### 3.1 The core

Loaded at every session start and after every compaction. It holds what bears on any turn.

1. **The standing goal.** Model what he knows and where his gaps are. Fill them with the few facts he needs to decide. Do not re-explain what he knows. The two hats. The coordinator's context is for him and the record: reading and long work go to workers, and the coordinator reads their reports. The profile of what he knows, once built, is read here.
2. **His role and his decisions.** He sets the goals and decides the design and process questions put to him. A bare go starts background work only; a batch needs his explicit go; a standing go covers what it names. What makes a decision consequential, and its three ways to him. A decision inside a worker's report is not made until he sees it. Search the record before asking him or measuring. A remark is not a decision, and a go is written nowhere. A deeper pass, not a halt or a rollback. Weigh a rule by its purpose and its cost. The coordinator's own proposal stays marked as its own until his yes. Any Fable worker beyond the standing pre-approvals needs his yes.
3. **Talking to him.** The register. The ask: what the work does, produces, touches and costs, what a yes commits him to and what a no costs; one ask per message, in the context its text gives; the recommendation last, in a line. Lists, not tables. Numbers as K or M, few, each with its meaning. A new term defined where it is used. A choice numbered. No dialog tool, a rule that lapses with the client. Time read from the clock, given in UTC and his time. Costs in tokens, writes only. Silence while a batch runs. Record edits: decision 11. The hook's reminders handled silently. While he reads turn by turn, restate each point in a line and hold it until he is done. No do-nothing option among the choices. Pages for him: a Select button per section, sources at the bottom, the house style, updated by URL after a compaction, a lost source rebuilt from the page. A push notification when he is away. A position's bold title is the record's handle, never quoted as his words.
4. **The facts of this environment.** His iPhone, Speak and dictation. A path does not open there; a page link or a GitHub URL does. His client can show stale state; the tree is the truth. His time zone. Compaction. A lost container keeps only what is pushed. Auto mode, the permission check and manual mode. The caches' lives: an hour for the session and a headless session, five minutes for a subagent. The platform's process stops. A message during a turn is queued; a stop kills the running agents. Cached reads are almost free. The tiers: workers on Opus, archaeology on Sonnet, Fable for a two-area judgement and the pre-approved reviews. The session's tier is his to set, for the register and the pool; the current tier is the boot note's.
5. **The record: what goes where.** Each home and its purpose: FACTS and POSITIONS (the project only, read in briefs), the history files, INDEX, PLAN, the boot note (the one home of state), the held list, the review queue, the notes and reports, the gap ledger, and the skills (how we work: this skill; rules that bind workers: `fortress-repo`; the platform: `cloud-container`). One home per thing. What he says about how we work comes here, refined. Push after every commit.
6. **The boot.** The boot order. What is read whole and what is looked up, which the trial boot settles. No directory listings; every output bounded. What is in flight, read from the tree. Whether a worker still runs: the harness's notice and its one output path. `git log`, one line. The boot note rewritten whole. After each start of the process, the git-check hook's reset, told to him in a line.
7. **The parts.** One line for each part: what it holds and when to load it.

### 3.2 The parts

Each is loaded when the coordinator switches into its work. Several can be loaded at once. No part restates another; it points.

1. **Delegating: briefing, launching, watching and resuming agents.** The briefer of workers. Loaded before the coordinator briefs, launches, watches, resumes or relaunches any agent, a batch's agents included. It holds the tiers, the Fable rule and the all-models pool; what a brief holds (the problem and not the answer, the research on file, the record's measurements as findings, the record's slice quoted and not restated, a length cap for an update, no second reader that reframes a document, no request that a worker cap its own spend, his rule quoted and never restated); watching a long run against its estimate, with check-ins armed at launch; waits and the prompt cache; interrupts and stops of the process; the Workflow's mechanics as their one home (a run resumed with the same script and arguments, a copy of the script as launched, the journal; `agent()` returning null; the async-body check); relaunching only at his ask; headless sessions; the scope of a second session (reviews on its own branch, not a batch or a change of route); a worker that builds a page pointed to the house CSS.
2. **Running and reviewing a batch.** The batch coordinator. Loaded when a batch is prepared, launched, watched, landed or reviewed. It holds the go a batch needs and the standing go's sequence; the workflow script and its manual, in scope for improvement; the base built once and the seeded worktrees; the roles (worker, skeptic, judge) and what each checks, the skeptic's reading of test-first from the transcript among them; no batch comparison of outputs and no baseline run; reversible stops, the blocking second review, tests-only repairs, and a deeper pass on a red gate; what a batch commits; the mission briefing; the checker-count and distance stages, citing POSITIONS "The checker count is measured, never red.", with `STAGE_BLIND` and the before tables; every masked difference and respelled line listed for him; the landing (consolidation, `revival-changes.md` updated, items listed for him); the review after every batch; when a batch resumes after a stop or the limits, pointing to Part 1 for how.
3. **Planning the road.** The roadmap architect. Loaded when PLAN's order or a phase is in question, before a batch is briefed, and when there is idle time. It holds PLAN's phases and parked items; a fork probed before a batch is briefed, named with the library's own way first; the nine steps; his answers asked in the plan's order, rows one per message with refreshers; idle time given to parked research; a new deliverable discussed with him first.
4. **Keeping the record.** The record-keeping part of the plan's step 2, with the record store's tool if he takes it. Loaded when the coordinator edits FACTS, POSITIONS, INDEX or a history file, folds a worker's report into the record, or runs a consolidation. It holds an entry's form and measure; the numbered entries; the history and its provenance; the pass after a worker finishes; the consolidation and its checks (nothing lost, the length check or a reader's, the quiz); INDEX's lines; the ledger as one file with derived views, its rows numbered for good, written only with `ledger.py`, a rewrite split among small workers after a duplicate search; a record that is public and names models on purpose. His open questions on the record's tooling and on the ledger's views shape it (HELD 7, 14, 15, 17, 19, 43, 80, 81). How workers read the record, and the edits a brief asks them to make, stay in `fortress-repo`.
5. **Rewriting a skill.** Loaded when a skill is to change, when the writer is briefed or resumed, when a cold read runs, and when his comments on a skill's page come in. It holds the outline first; the `fortress-repo` method, and the heavier method of this rewrite; the seven writing principles and the register; the headless writer, resumed or started fresh; the cold read, the coordinator's review of its flags, and his reading of whole parts; a comment marks a problem area; the writer's minor decisions settled by the coordinator; a check that the skill caught his meaning; `revival-changes.md` kept current; a rewrite no longer than what it replaces; the skills' split, pointing to Core 5.
6. **Analysis: process engineering and post-mortems.** The analyst. Loaded when the coordinator measures what the work costs or how long it takes, tests a change to the process, or finds out what happened and why. It holds where the work's costs are measured; the spend read from the transcripts' usage records; a boot's cost and the tokens per byte; the Fable ratio; the development loop as a first-class concern; small tests on the records at hand; archaeology by Sonnet scouts; reading transcripts and Workflow journals; the post-mortem's index into a transcript; the profile of what he knows, built here as its own task; the open experiments he named (HELD 108, 113, 115, 118).

1. POSITIONS 102, "Test first, the test kept.": leaves in part. Stays: the first sentence and the one-commit sentence, in "The suites and the gate". Leaves: the skeptic's reading from the transcript, to Part 2. The worker rule is already in `tests-writing.md`.

14. The counts: "How we work" keeps 5 of 35, two whole and three in part, in "The suites and the gate"; "The one library and the compiled checker" keeps 25 of 26.

## 4. The writer's brief, and the plan's decisions

### 4.1 What the brief (the plan's section 3) must change

- **Point 2.** The rule texts are POSITIONS's two conduct sections as they stand, not as consolidated; the protocol; the 3 entries and 5 clauses that leave POSITIONS from other sections, with the clauses of 102 and 103; the 2 FACTS clauses; the 26 container entries and the ledger entry; and the held list's 23 rules and 32 questions, each with its home. ### 4.2 The decisions (the plan's section 4) the outline changes

Each with the default I recommend.

- **Decision 6, the modes.** The outline's six parts replace the brief's seven candidates. Default: take them; the writer may merge or split with a reason.
- **Decision 7, the five rules.** All five now have a home: the reversible stop in Part 2, the fork in Part 3, FACTS whole, the bounded boot and in-flight-from-the-tree in Core 6. Default unchanged: keep all five.
